title: Bài sưu tầm 119 - Passage 1: The Ginkgo Biloba: The Resilient Living Fossil
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 119

The Ginkgo Biloba: The Resilient Living Fossil

Paragraph 1. Possessing fan-shaped leaves that turn a radiant golden hue each autumn, the ginkgo tree (Ginkgo biloba), or maidenhair tree, is a botanical marvel. As the sole surviving representative of the Ginkgoales—an ancient taxonomic order of gymnosperms that flourished alongside the dinosaurs during the Jurassic epoch roughly 170 million years ago—the ginkgo is frequently celebrated as a 'living fossil'. While hundreds of related prehistoric species known from the fossil record were extinguished during the late Cretaceous mass extinction, Ginkgo biloba survived virtually unchanged in morphological structure, its contemporary leaf veins and cellular architecture mirroring specimens preserved in rock formations millions of years old.

Paragraph 2. By the seventeenth century, Western botanists assumed that the entire ginkgo lineage had vanished into evolutionary history. That scientific assumption was overturned in 1691, when German physician and explorer Engelbert Kaempfer, stationed on a diplomatic outpost in Japan, visited ancient Buddhist monasteries and discovered magnificent, living ginkgo trees flourishing in temple courtyards. For centuries, Chinese and Japanese monks had preserved the species from extinction, regarding the trees as sacred symbols of longevity, cosmic balance, and enlightenment. Monks cultivated groves around their mountain sanctuaries and prized the timber for sacred carpentry, recognizing that the wood possessed exceptional fire-retardant qualities that shielded temple complexes during forest blazes.

Paragraph 3. Botanically, the ginkgo is a dioecious species, meaning individual trees are either strictly male or female. Unlike modern conifers that package their seeds in cones, female ginkgos produce naked, fleshy seeds hanging in pairs on long stalks. When these plum-like seeds ripen and drop to the earth in late autumn, their fleshy outer coating—the sarcotesta—decomposes rapidly, releasing concentrated quantities of butyric and hexanoic acids. These volatile compounds generate an overwhelming, rancid stench remarkably similar to sour butter or rotting meat. For this reason, municipal landscaping agencies worldwide rigorously avoid planting female specimens along city streets, opting exclusively to propagate cloned male saplings through tissue cuttings.

Paragraph 4. The biological longevity of individual ginkgo trees, which routinely live for more than one thousand years, is underpinned by extraordinary chemical defenses. The wood and leaves synthesize an array of unique chemical compounds, including ginkgolides and bilobalides, alongside potent flavonoids that repel insect pests, neutralize destructive fungal rots, and inhibit bacterial infections. Furthermore, the tree possesses deep, anchoring taproots that impart incredible structural resistance against hurricane-force winds, while its cellular tissues demonstrate an astonishing tolerance to high concentrations of modern urban air pollutants, such as sulphur dioxide and ozone.

Paragraph 5. The ginkgo’s legendary resilience was tested to its ultimate extreme on 6 August 1945, when an atomic bomb was detonated over the Japanese city of Hiroshima. The catastrophic nuclear explosion, which unleashed extreme blast shockwaves and incinerated everything within a two-kilometre radius, scorched six mature ginkgo trees standing near local shrines. While nearby stone buildings crumbled and wooden structures turned to ash, the subterranean root networks of these charred trees survived. The following spring, without any visible genetic mutations or stunted growth, the damaged trunks sprouted vigorous green buds. Today, these six historic trees remain alive in Hiroshima, venerated as living monuments to survival. Paradoxically, while cloned ginkgos are cultivated in millions across urban capitals worldwide, wild populations are critically endangered, restricted to isolated mountainous reserves in China’s Zhejiang province.

steps: Đoạn 1: Cây ginkgo sống sót gần như không thay đổi cấu trúc hình thái (virtually unchanged in morphological structure, its contemporary leaf veins... mirroring specimens preserved in rock formations).

q9.text: Chinese monks sold ginkgo timber to European merchants during the seventeenth century.

steps: Đoạn 2: Có nhắc đến việc các nhà sư dùng gỗ để làm đồ mộc thờ cúng, nhưng không hề đề cập có bán gỗ cho thương nhân châu Âu hay không.
